prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with the gamma-ray burst afterglows (B010) because the instrument story is close to my own work, but the opening ballots show that nobody else shares that ranking, and when I weigh the evidence rather than my own taste, the optical lattice clock is the strongest candidate on the table. It is a measurement instrument that did something concrete: the magic-wavelength idea removed the trade-off between trapping many atoms and perturbing the clock transition, and the realisation in strontium took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. That is the most precise measurement ever made by anyone. It already supports tests of the gravitational redshift at millimetre scales, searches for variation of constants and relativistic geodesy, and it is at the centre of the discussion on redefining the second. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reproduce and compare these clocks routinely, which is exactly the independent confirmation I ask of any claim. The attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first realisations, Ye for driving the platform to record accuracy and stability. Three members ranked it first and a fourth second, and those include the atomic-physics specialists who can judge the details better than I can.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is lineage and timing. The frequency comb prize of 2005 and the ion-trap clock work recognised in 2012 sit very close to this field, so a citation must be framed narrowly around the lattice concept, or the committee will be accused of rewarding a refinement of earlier prizes. Other groups (Lemonde, Hollberg, Gill and NIST colleagues) can argue a share, and a two-person prize leaves them out. The practical payoff, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, so one can argue the prize should wait for it. Finally, I ranked this sixth in my own opening ballot, and I am moving it up on the strength of colleagues' expertise in a field that is not mine, which is a real limit on how firmly I hold the position.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the optical lattice clock first as a textbook precision-measurement advance with a clean two-person attribution, and he put ultracold-atom quantum simulation second.
responses.response: I agree on the clock and have moved my vote towards it. I disagree mildly on pairing it with B012, because that would take us past three people, and Kroll himself notes the four-name problem there. I would also press him on the 2012 and 2005 overlap: what exactly is the claim that is new and not already credited to the comb and ion-clock prizes? If the answer is the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom stability gain, I am comfortable.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the clock first because she can judge the atomic physics directly, the agreement between laboratories is exceptional, and the work builds on earlier comb and laser-cooling prizes.
responses.response: Her point that the physics is clear and independently confirmed carries more weight with me than my own opening ranking. Where I qualify her is on the lineage: building on earlier prizes is a strength for the physics but a risk for the citation, so I would want the wording to name the lattice clock and not 'precision spectroscopy' in general. I would also like her to say whether she thinks Lemonde or others have a stronger claim than I gave them credit for.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, valuing the theory-to-experiment link and the lasting impact on quantum materials, and judged the discovery robust even though the pairing mechanism is debated.
responses.response: I take his case seriously, and B009 is my first alternative: many groups reproduced the correlated phases and the Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero pair is a natural theory plus experiment split. My reservation is attribution and maturity, not merit. Cao and the other first authors, Cory Dean's group and earlier flat-band theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres) are all open questions, and Johansson, Lindroth and Mehlig all describe the superconductivity as unsettled. I cannot judge the condensed-matter details and ask him to say which part of the discovery is settled enough to cite without the pairing mechanism.

responses.point: Olsson ranked twisted bilayer graphene first and the lattice clock second, wanting the historical record checked for related earlier theory and for the roles of co-first authors.
responses.response: I agree that the record needs checking, and that is why I do not treat the three-name B009 trio as obviously fixed. On the other hand, her ranking shows that the clock is acceptable to both camps, which matters to me as Chair. I am not trying to manufacture consensus, but a candidate that both the atomic specialists and a first-place condensed-matter voter rate in their top two deserves to be treated as a serious compromise.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the IceCube neutrino discovery first as a discovery from nature that opened a new window, and noted that credit to a single laureate under-represents collaborators and AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND.
responses.response: I share his view that neutrino astronomy opens a real window, and I ranked B047 second, so it stays as an alternative. But we also agree on the weakness: a single name for a collaboration of hundreds, and a source-identification story that rests on one blazar association and a Galactic-plane map. I would not put a one-person prize on the table until we can say who else belongs, and the shortlist does not give me that. I also note he put the gravitational-wave background last on his list as premature, which matches my own reading.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked active-matter hydrodynamics first as a clear and universal account of collective motion with a natural Vicsek, Toner-Tu and Ramaswamy trio.
responses.response: The theory is elegant and has stood for thirty years, and I respect the argument that a simple mechanism explains messy systems. My difficulty is that the shortlist shows no other member ranking it at all, and he himself says quantitative tests of the exponents are only partial. As an experimentalist I would want to know which decisive measurement confirms the Toner-Tu prediction, and I would ask him to explain why this should rank above fields with many independent confirmations. I do not rule it out, but I do not see how it reaches a consensus.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants a lattice-clock citation framed narrowly enough to avoid overlap with the 2005 frequency comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
Whether Lemonde, Hollberg or other lattice-clock contributors have a claim that makes a two-person prize look incomplete.

Whether the twisted bilayer graphene prize is better now or later, given the unsettled superconducting mechanism, and whether the credit should include Cao and other first authors; I defer to condensed-matter colleagues.
Whether a single-laureate neutrino prize can be defended without naming other IceCube and AMANDA leaders, and how firm the source identification is.
My own opening ranking of the clock sixth was formed with less expertise than that of the atomic-physics colleagues, so I may be over-weighting their agreement.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, which are adjacent to the gamma-ray burst and astroparticle candidates (B010, B047), and I opened by ranking B010 first, so I should be careful about that field if it returns, but I have no personal or institutional tie to any credited person on the shortlist that I can identify.
